thought.text: The `pkill` matched my own shell again (bracket trick applies only to the pattern, not my command text). Let me redo with safe patterns:

reasoning_content:
It's highly likely that pkill killed my shell again (pkill -f 'docker buil[d]'... no wait, that's not it. The problem is pkill -f 'wave2.s[h]'... hmm. Actually, what matched was probably... my own shell's command line contains the literal string 'wave2.s[h]' — pkill -f matches against the full command line of processes. Since the bash -lc wrapper contains my full command string, pkill matched it and killed it. That's exactly why earlier I got exit 143 and no output came out.

I need to use a pattern that doesn't match my own command line. For example, use `pkill -f 'wave2\.sh'` while making sure my command doesn't literally contain 'wave2\.sh'... but it still ends up containing it in the same command. A better approach: use a variable/indirect pattern, or use pgrep to match only the actual script path and filter out my own PID. The simplest is: `pkill -f "build-logs/wave2\.sh"` — but my command line also contains this string. Use the bracket trick in a way that doesn't match: the actual process's command line is `/bin/bash .build-logs/wave2.sh` (or nohup). Use the pattern 'wave2[.]sh' — my command line contains the literal "wave2[.]sh" (with the brackets), and this does NOT match the regex 'wave2[.]sh' (which matches "wave2.sh"). Because the literal text in my command is 'wave2[.]sh' (with brackets), which doesn't match the regex. And the actual process has "wave2.sh", which does match. This is the standard trick.

Also, check whether the sed was executed. Let me try running the steps separately.

action.command: pkill -f 'wave2[.]sh' 2>/dev/null; pkill -f 'docker bui[l]d' 2>/dev/null; sleep 2; ps aux | grep -cE '[w]ave2[.]sh|[d]ocker bui' ; grep -c 'prompt-security' /workspace/.build-logs/wave2.sh 2>/dev/null || echo "sed not applied"
